title: Ancient Pirates and Rome's Answer
description: Caesar's ransom, Pompey's 89-day sweep and who counted as a pirate

concepts.title: The Captive Who Raised His Own Ransom
concepts.contentHtml:
Picture a young Roman aristocrat crossing the Aegean to study rhetoric on Rhodes. In 75 BCE, near the little island of Pharmacusa, pirates from Cilicia, on the southern coast of what is now Turkey, seized his ship.1 The captive was Julius Caesar, then about twenty-five, and what happened next became one of antiquity's favourite stories.

According to Plutarch, when the pirates demanded twenty talents for his ransom, Caesar laughed at them for not knowing who they had caught and offered fifty instead.2 He sent his companions off to raise the money and stayed for thirty-eight days with one friend and two attendants. He joined the pirates' games, wrote poems and speeches and read them aloud, called anyone who failed to admire them an illiterate barbarian, and laughingly threatened to hang them all. The pirates put it down to boyish high spirits.

Once the ransom arrived from Miletus, Caesar manned ships, caught his captors still at anchor off the island and took their money. When the governor of Asia dithered, apparently eyeing the loot, Caesar took the prisoners out of the jail at Pergamum and crucified them all, just as he had promised. Suetonius adds a twist: he presents Caesar as merciful, because he ordered their throats cut before they were crucified.3

How far should you trust this? Plutarch lived from about 45 to 125 CE, well over a century after the kidnapping. The two writers disagree on small details (thirty-eight days in Plutarch, nearly forty in Suetonius), and the tale flatters Caesar perfectly: cool, witty and as good as his word. Treat it as a well-attested legend about a real kidnapping, and notice what it takes for granted. In the 70s BCE, Plutarch says, pirates already controlled the sea with large armaments and countless small vessels, and they were organised enough to hold a Roman noble for weeks while the money came.

concepts.title: Pompey's Eighty-Nine Days
concepts.contentHtml:
Caesar's captors were part of a much bigger problem. The Cilician pirates were not all from Cilicia: they were men of many nationalities who used its hidden coves and timber-rich hills as a base. Their power grew after Rome defeated the Seleucid Empire, which controlled part of the region, in 190 BCE, and Rome was slow to act, partly because pirates were useful. They supplied slaves, and Roman traders turned the island of Delos into one of the most infamous slave markets in the region.

They were also unreliable partners. In 70 BCE the rebel Spartacus paid them to ferry his army to Sicily; they took the money and never turned up.1 By 67 BCE pirates had sacked Ostia, Rome's own port, and Plutarch claims they had more than a thousand ships and had captured four hundred cities. Worst of all, they preyed on the grain ships that fed Rome.

That year the lex Gabinia (Gabinian Law) gave Pompey the Great an extraordinary command against the pirates for three years. The senator Quintus Lutatius Catulus objected that Pompey was too eminent for comfort in a free republic and that all power should not be placed in one man's hands. He arguably had a point: commands like this one helped teach Romans to accept the rule of a single strongman.

Pompey needed nowhere near three years. He divided the Mediterranean into thirteen districts, each with its own fleet and commander, and as each district was cleared its ships joined the next sweep.2 The last pirates were beaten at Coracesium off the Cilician coast, and the whole job took a reported 89 days.3 Then came the surprise. Instead of crucifying or beheading his prisoners, Pompey resettled many of them on farmland in lowland Cilicia, at places such as Soli, which became Pompeiopolis. Piracy was a way of making a living, and giving men a better one on land proved as useful as sinking their ships.

concepts.title: Robber or Emperor? Who Counts as a Pirate
concepts.contentHtml:
The English word goes back to the Greek peiráomai, "to attempt", which shifted into a Greek word for a brigand and then into the Latin pirata. What it named was not always shameful. The Athenian historian Thucydides says that early Greeks raided unwalled towns for a living, with no disgrace attached and even some glory.1 In the old poems, he adds, people casually asked arriving sailors whether they were pirates, and nobody took offence at the question.

States used pirates and behaved like them. In 355 BCE three Athenian ambassadors sailing to Caria made their captain chase a merchant ship from Naucratis in Egypt and seized its cargo. When the orator Demosthenes attacked them, his complaint was not the seizure, since Athens was at war with Egypt, but that they kept the loot instead of handing it to the state. Queen Teuta of the Illyrians encouraged her subjects' raiding as long as the victims were foreigners.

Saint Augustine told the story of a captured pirate brought before Alexander the Great and asked what he meant by keeping hostile possession of the sea. The pirate replied that he did the same as Alexander, "but because I do it with a petty ship, I am called a robber, while you who does it with a great fleet are styled emperor.2" The retort still stings, because it asks the question this topic keeps returning to: is a pirate defined by what he does, or by who has authorised it?

Roman law gave one answer. Cicero argued that a promise of ransom made to pirates need not be kept, even under oath,3 because a pirate is not a lawful enemy but "the common foe of all the world". An ordinary enemy belonged to a state you could make treaties with; a pirate belonged to none. That idea, later compressed into the Latin tag hostis humani generis, "enemy of the human race", still shapes the law of the sea, as the final lesson shows.

title: Raiders of the Baltic and the China Seas
description: The Victual Brothers, Störtebeker's skull, the wokou and the Ming sea ban

concepts.title: The Victual Brothers: Hired Help Gone Rogue
concepts.contentHtml:
Piracy did not need the Mediterranean sun. In the late fourteenth century a war between Denmark and Sweden, with Queen Margaret of Denmark on one side and her rival Albert on the other, drew freelance fighters into the Baltic. Albert's side hired them to attack Danish ships and keep the besieged city of Stockholm supplied, and in the winter of 1393–94 a small fleet of them ran provisions in. Because they mostly fed themselves as they went, they became known as the Vitalienbrüder or Victual Brothers: Vitalien is an old word for food.

When peace came the following year, they kept going, because raiding paid too well to stop. From a base on Gotland in the middle of the Baltic they attacked Hanseatic merchant ships as well as Danish ones, until in 1398 the Teutonic Order, allied with the Hansa, drove them out. Many fled to the North Sea, where feuding Frisian chieftains were glad to hire experienced fighters. You will meet this pattern again and again: war creates licensed raiders, and peace leaves them armed and unemployed.

Their most famous captain, Klaus Störtebeker, owes his fame mostly to legend. His name is old German for "tip up the mug", after his fabled drinking. Hamburg's ships caught him off Heligoland, and he was beheaded with dozens of his men; accounts range from about thirty to seventy. The best-known tale says he asked that every comrade his headless body could walk past be spared. Legend has it that his corpse staggered past eleven men before it fell, and Hamburg executed them anyway.1 Even the year is disputed: tradition says 1401, while Hamburg's own history site argues for October 1400.

In 1878 builders found a skull pierced by a large rusty nail in an area where pirates had once been beheaded and their heads displayed on spikes.2 Hamburg's history museum long displayed it as Störtebeker's. Forensic work suggests it belonged to a man beheaded around 1400, though not necessarily him, and a 2004 attempt to match its DNA with possible descendants failed.3 In January 2010 someone stole it.

concepts.title: Wokou: The Raiders of Korea's Coasts
concepts.contentHtml:
At the other end of Eurasia, Chinese records spoke of the wokou, Koreans of the waegu and Japanese of the wakō. All three are versions of one term for Japanese pirates, and the characters carry an insult: World History Encyclopedia translates them as "dwarf pirates". Raiders had plundered East Asian shipping since at least the eighth century, but the wokou of the thirteenth century onwards went further, helped by the disruption to legitimate trade that followed the Mongol invasions of Korea between 1231 and 1259.

Their most notorious base was Tsushima, a rocky, mountainous island between Korea and Japan where people struggled to grow enough food and the local Sō lords profited from sponsoring raids. Iki Island and Matsura were others. At their fourteenth-century peak, hundreds of pirate ships worked the straits and made four or five major raids on southern Korea a year. Raiding parties of up to 3,000 men sailed in fleets of up to 400 ships.1 They stole anything of value, especially bulk goods such as cloth, grain and rice, and they took people to sell as slaves, so that many farming communities withdrew inland and abandoned their best land.

Korea fought back with technology and force. In 1380 Choe Muson, who had worked tirelessly to develop gunpowder, used ship-borne cannon to defeat a large pirate fleet at the mouth of the Kum River.2 Korean forces attacked Tsushima itself in 1389 and again in 1419, when 700 suspected pirates were executed. Force alone did not work, so Korea tried economics. In 1443 the Treaty of Kyehae opened legitimate trade between Tsushima and three Korean ports, removing part of the pirates' income, until disturbances by Japanese traders wrecked it in 1510 and raids returned.

The deepest lesson hides in the name. "Japanese pirates" described a reputation, not a passport. The label was applied to raiders from Japan, Korea, China and later Portugal, and some pirates even disguised themselves as Japanese to hide where they had really sailed from.3

concepts.title: The Ming Sea Ban: How a Ban Made Pirates
concepts.contentHtml:
China's answer under the Ming dynasty was defence and prohibition. Hunting pirates across vast seas seemed hopeless; the Yongle Emperor complained that ships could not readily reach them, "nor could spears or arrows readily touch them." So the Ming built forts along the most vulnerable coasts and banned private maritime trade altogether. The logic was neat: if no unofficial ship may sail, any unofficial ship is a pirate.

The result was the opposite of what was intended. Demand for trade did not vanish because it was forbidden, so merchants became smugglers and smugglers armed themselves. By the sixteenth century many wokou, perhaps even the majority, were Chinese, many of them former traders angry at Ming restrictions and taxes on trade.1 They worked alongside Japanese crews and Portuguese traders, who often collaborated with pirates to smuggle goods into China. The most wanted leader, Wang Zhi (written Wang Chih in older books), was captured in 1557.

The Ming eventually paired force with fiscal reform. A new tax system let subjects pay in silver instead of doing military service, and the revenue paid for a coastal navy. The generals Hu Zongxian and Qi Jiguang (Hu Tsung-hsien and Chi Chi-kuang in older spellings) inflicted serious defeats on the pirates. In Japan the warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi, once he had unified the centre of the country, tried something cleverer: from 1592 he let former pirates trade legitimately as long as they carried his personal red seal.2 These became the shuin-sen, the "red seal ships". Turning raiders into licensed traders worked better than chasing them, although Hideyoshi also used former wako and their ships in his invasion of Korea from 1592.

Piracy in Chinese waters did not end there. From 1807 to 1810 Zheng Yi Sao led a vast pirate confederation in the South China Sea, a story told in the Strange History topic. The wokou preview this topic's central theme: whether a sailor counts as a pirate, a smuggler, a trader or a servant of the state often depends on who writes the rules.

title: The Barbary Corsairs
description: Barbarossa's Algiers, raids on Iceland and Ireland, and the fight over the numbers

concepts.title: Corsair States: Barbarossa's Algiers
concepts.contentHtml:
From the sixteenth century the most feared raiders in European waters sailed from North Africa's Barbary Coast. Morocco was an independent kingdom; Algiers, Tunis and Tripoli owed a loose allegiance to the Ottoman Empire.1 Their raiding was state-supported piracy, used to take ships and captives and to make weaker sea powers pay tribute for safe passage. Europeans called these raiders corsairs.

The model was built by two brothers from the Greek island of Lesbos, sons of a Christian renegade who had joined the Ottoman army. In 1503 the elder, Oruç, was captured by the Knights Hospitaller, a Christian military order then based on Rhodes, and spent two terrible years as a galley slave before escaping.2 Christian powers ran slave galleys too. In 1516 the emir of Algiers asked Oruç to help expel Spanish soldiers from a nearby island fortress. Oruç took the city for himself, and the emir was apparently drowned in his bath. His nickname, Baba Oruç ("Father Oruç"), sounded to Italian ears like barba rossa, "red beard", and he did have one.

When Oruç died in 1518, his brother Hayreddin inherited both Algiers and the nickname Barbarossa, though his own hair was golden brown. Under Spanish pressure he sought the help of the Ottoman sultan Süleyman the Magnificent, who made him admiral in chief of the Ottoman fleet. In 1538 at Preveza in Greece he defeated a stronger fleet under the Genoese admiral Andrea Doria, and in 1546 he died peacefully in Istanbul. A pirate had become an empire's admiral.

The economy behind it ran on people. Captives were sold, put to work or held for ransom. Ruling pashas were entitled to an eighth of all captured Christians,3 whom they housed in overcrowded prisons called baños ("baths") and used for public works such as building harbours. Ransoming became an industry in Christian Europe: the Trinitarian order, founded in 1198, existed to buy captives back.

concepts.title: From Algiers to Iceland and Ireland
concepts.contentHtml:
Corsairs did not stay in the Mediterranean. In 1627 twelve ships left Algiers, and four headed for Iceland. On 20 June one landed at Grindavík and took twelve Icelanders and three Danes. On 4 July two ships raided the eastern fjords, taking about a hundred Icelanders and a dozen Danes. On 16 July they reached Vestmannaeyjar, the Westman Islands, where they killed between thirty and forty people and took 242 prisoners.1 The captives were sold as slaves in Algiers.

Icelanders still call it the Tyrkjaránið, the "Turkish Raid", though the raiders came from Algiers, then part of the Ottoman world. The pastor Ólafur Egilsson was freed to ask King Christian IV of Denmark to pay ransom, and later wrote an account of his ordeal. Ten years after the raid, twenty-seven captives came home, ransomed with money raised by taxes and donations.2 Most never returned.

Four years later corsairs struck Ireland. On 17 June 1631 two ships from Algiers, one a 300-ton Dutch-built warship with 24 guns, captured a ship from Dartmouth and then two fishing boats from Dungarvan. Their commander, Morat Rais, a Dutch convert to Islam, ordered one fisherman, John Hackett, to pilot them into Kinsale.3 Hackett, perhaps aware that a Royal Navy ship lay there, steered them to Baltimore in west Cork instead. The Dutch-built ships, and perhaps friendly flags, fooled observers. At 2 a.m. on 20 June some 230 armed men landed and seized about a hundred people;4 when the ships sailed they held 154 captives in all.

England had just adopted a policy of refusing ransoms, believing that paying encouraged hostage-taking, so the money never came, and few of the Baltimore captives can be shown to have been redeemed. Hackett was condemned to death at the Cork assizes. Baltimore is the only recorded corsair slaving raid in Ireland, and History Ireland notes that Icelandic narratives of a 1627 raid led by Morat Rais even remember his crew's kindness to children.

concepts.title: How Many Captives? The Fight Over a Number
concepts.contentHtml:
How many Europeans did the corsairs enslave? Nobody kept reliable totals, and older studies, counting captives in one city or one period, mostly arrived at thousands or at most tens of thousands. The Ohio State University historian Robert Davis turned the problem upside down in his book Christian Slaves, Muslim Masters.

His method was indirect. Davis took the best records of how many slaves were held in a given place at one time, then estimated how many new captives were needed to replace those who died, escaped, converted or were ransomed. If roughly a quarter had to be replaced annually to keep the population stable, as it apparently was between 1580 and 1680, the corsairs must have taken about 8,500 people a year,1 nearly a million in that century, plus as many as 475,000 in the periods before and after. His conclusion: between 1530 and 1780 almost certainly a million, and quite possibly 1.25 million, European Christians were enslaved on the Barbary Coast. Davis admitted it was "not the best way to make population estimates, but it is the only way with the limited records available."

Historians split. The economic historian Ian Blanchard said the numbers appeared to add up. David Earle, author of The Pirate Wars, argued that Davis may have erred by extrapolating from 1580 to 1680, the most intense slaving period,2 and warned that corsairs also seized non-Christian eastern Europeans and black West Africans. The weak point is structural: a total built on assumed replacement rates multiplies any error in them across 250 years.

Two facts keep the figure in proportion. Even the high estimate is small beside the Atlantic slave trade, which carried about 10 to 12 million Africans to the Americas. And enslavement ran both ways: in a later book Davis estimated that more than a million Muslims were enslaved in Europe,3 coining the term "faith slavery". He has also had to push back against people online who use his figure to excuse Atlantic slavery, calling it a "misuse" of his work.

title: Privateers: Pirates with Paperwork
description: Letters of marque, Drake, the buccaneers, Kidd and the 1856 ban

concepts.title: Licensed to Plunder: Drake and the Letter of Marque
concepts.contentHtml:
Between the pirate and the navy stood a third figure, the privateer: a private captain commissioned by a government to attack its enemies. The commission was a letter of marque, also called a letter of reprisal. As the historian Robert Blyth puts it, in wartime British captains might be given a letter of marque which allowed them to intercept enemy shipping and thereby disrupt trade. The reward was prize money from whatever they captured. The danger, Blyth adds, was that habits learned in wartime could easily give way to peacetime piracy.

The Elizabethan sea dogs show how blurred the line could be. Francis Drake raided Spain's American empire at a time when England was not officially at war with Spain, so he could not yet receive a letter of marque. In 1572 he seized silver in huge quantities from a treasure caravan at Nombre de Dios in Panama. On his voyage of 1577–1580 the Golden Hind, the only one of his five ships to sail right round the world, captured a Spanish treasure ship so rich that transferring the loot took days. To the Spanish he was a pirate, feared as1 el Draque, "the dragon". Elizabeth I, a shareholder in the voyage, saw a hero, and she knighted him on board the ship in April 1581.2

How much did it matter? In 1930 the economist John Maynard Keynes made a startling claim:3 "I trace the beginnings of British foreign investment to the treasure which Drake stole from Spain in 1580." Out of her share, he wrote, Elizabeth paid off England's entire foreign debt, balanced her budget and still had about £40,000, which she invested in the Levant Company, whose profits helped found the East India Company. By Keynes's arithmetic, every pound Drake brought home had become £100,000.

Read it as Keynes meant it: an illustration of compound interest, not an audited history. But it captures something true about the age. State-licensed plunder was a business with shareholders, and the Crown was one of them.

concepts.title: Buccaneers, a Knight and a Hanged Privateer
concepts.contentHtml:
The word buccaneer began with barbecue. From 1620 European hunters camped illegally on the western end of Hispaniola, smoking meat on a grill over a fire of dung and green twigs.1 The French called them boucaniers, from an Arawak word, bukan. Remembering Spanish attacks on their camps, many turned to raiding Spanish ships and towns from havens such as Tortuga. The name spread after 1684, when The Buccaneers of America, a popular history by the Dutchman Alexandre Exquemelin, himself a former buccaneer, appeared in English.

After England captured Jamaica from Spain in 1655, its governors encouraged buccaneers of every nationality to operate from Port Royal and issued them letters of marque, so strictly speaking the buccaneers were privateers. The greatest was the Welshman Henry Morgan. In 1668 he took the treasure port of Portobelo, and in January 1671, with up to 2,000 men in 33 ships, he captured Panama, which burned to the ground. But England and Spain had just made peace in the Treaty of Madrid, and the news took a year to reach the Caribbean. Morgan was arrested and sent to London in 1672. In 1674 Charles II knighted him and sent him back to Jamaica as lieutenant governor.2

Captain William Kidd had the opposite luck. In 1696 he sailed with a commission signed by William III, backed by the Earl of Bellomont, the new governor of New York and Massachusetts, and anonymous London investors, to hunt French ships and pirates in the Indian Ocean. Rich prizes were scarce and his crew grew mutinous; in 1697 he killed his gunner, William Moore, reportedly with a wooden bucket. In 1698 he took the Quedah Merchant, which carried French passes. But the war with France had ended months earlier, and his backers, keen to hide their interest, abandoned him. Key documents, including the French passes, went missing.3 Kidd was hanged at Wapping on 23 May 1701, and the first rope snapped. Morgan and Kidd did similar things; timing and politics made one a knight and the other a corpse.

concepts.title: Abolishing the Privateer
concepts.contentHtml:
Privateering outlived the buccaneers by more than a century. The United States Constitution gives Congress the power1 "To declare War, grant Letters of Marque and Reprisal, and make Rules concerning Captures on Land and Water", and bars the individual states from granting such letters. The clause is still there. Prize money drew Americans into privateering during the War of Independence and the War of 1812. The War of 1812 was the last time the United States commissioned privateers.2

Europe's great powers moved to end the practice. At the Congress of Paris, in the wake of the Crimean War, they adopted the Declaration of Paris on 16 April 1856. Its first article was blunt: "Privateering is and remains abolished."3 The others set rules for neutral shipping. A neutral flag protects enemy goods except contraband of war; neutral goods under an enemy flag cannot be seized; and a blockade binds only if it is effective, enforced by a force strong enough really to prevent access to the coast. The declaration bound only the powers that acceded to it.

The United States refused to sign. Privateers, it argued, were necessary for a nation without a strong navy.4 Secretary of State William Marcy offered to give them up only if the powers went further and exempted all private property at sea from capture by warships, a condition known as the Marcy amendment. Even so, the United States accepted the declaration's rules in practice during the Civil War and the Spanish–American War, and when the Civil War began in April 1861 it was the Confederate president, Jefferson Davis, who called for privateers to attack Union commerce.

Why did privateering fade? States built permanent navies that could do the job themselves, and privateers were hard to control. As Morgan and Kidd showed, the line between privateer and pirate was a matter of paperwork, timing and politics. Once governments kept violence at sea for their own navies, anyone raiding without a commission was simply a pirate.

title: The Golden Age: Blackbeard, Black Bart and Pirate Democracy
description: Blackbeard's wreck, Roberts's articles and two readings of shipboard democracy

concepts.title: Blackbeard: The Man, the Legend and the Wreck
concepts.contentHtml:
The pirates everyone pictures come from a short window that historians date differently, from roughly 1650 to 1730 in one common definition or the 1680s to the 1720s in another. Its most famous face is Blackbeard, and the striking thing is how little is known about him. Even his real name is uncertain, usually given as some form of Edward Thatch or Teach. The earliest document that names him dates from the summer of 1717, and he was dead by the end of 1718.

That short career was spectacular. Late in 1717, near Martinique, his men captured the French slave ship La Concorde and kept it as his flagship, renamed Queen Anne's Revenge. In May 1718 he blockaded Charleston, South Carolina, for nearly a week and held prisoners. His ransom demand was not gold but a chest of medicine.1 In June the flagship ran aground at what is now Beaufort Inlet, North Carolina; a former captive claimed Blackbeard did it on purpose to break up a company of more than 300 pirates. In November a force led by Lieutenant Robert Maynard killed him at Ocracoke Inlet and sailed home with his head hanging from the bowsprit.

The fearsome image owes much to Charles Johnson's 1724 General History of the Pyrates, which gave him fourteen wives where the records show one legal marriage. There is no evidence that he tortured or mistreated his captives.2 Terror was a brand: if victims surrendered at the sight of him, nobody had to fight.

The wreck turned legend into evidence. On 21 November 1996 searchers from the private firm Intersal found cannon and anchors near Beaufort Inlet,3 and more than 400,000 artefacts have been raised since. The oddest came from a breech-loading cannon chamber cleaned in 2016: sixteen paper scraps, none larger than a small coin. One italicised word, "Hilo", led researchers to the Peruvian port of Ilo and then to the 1712 first edition of Captain Edward Cooke4's A Voyage to the South Sea. Someone aboard had owned a travel book, and its pages ended up stuffed into a gun.

concepts.title: Black Bart's Articles
concepts.contentHtml:
By numbers, the most successful pirate of the age was not Blackbeard but a Welshman, Bartholomew Roberts, born in Pembrokeshire in 1682 with the first name John. In February 1720 he joined, willingly or not, the crew of the Welsh pirate Howell Davis, and changed his first name to make himself harder to trace. In a career of about three years he plundered more than 400 ships on both sides of the Atlantic.1 Curiously, he never drank alcohol; his favourite drink was tea.

Roberts ran his ships by written articles, a contract every member swore to. Johnson printed eleven of them, and they read more like a club rulebook than a robbers' charter. The first began: "Every Man has a Vote in the Affairs of Moment".2 Lights and candles were to be put out at eight o'clock at night, and anyone who wanted to keep drinking had to do it on the open deck. A man who lost a limb or was disabled was to receive 800 pieces of eight, with smaller sums for lesser injuries.

Rules for the crew did not mean mercy for others. In October 1720 Roberts ordered his men to cut the ears off a group of Dutch captives. His end came off Cape Lopez, in modern Gabon. On 9 February 1722 his crew celebrated a capture by drinking through the ship's liquor, and the next day HMS Swallow under Captain Chaloner Ogle tracked them down. Roberts chose to fight and was killed by grapeshot that tore out his throat. At the trial at Cape Coast Castle, in modern Ghana, 72 men were sentenced to death: 52 were hanged and 20 were sent to seven years3' labour in West African mines. Ogle became the only naval officer knighted for an anti-piracy operation.

Where do such articles come from? Mostly from Johnson's book and from trial records, so it is fair to ask how typical they were. But other crews' codes survive too, including George Lowther's and the 1724 articles of John Phillips's Revenge, which also compensated men for lost limbs.

concepts.title: Democracy at Sea? Two Readings
concepts.contentHtml:
Pirate ships look startlingly democratic. Crews elected their captains and could depose them. Power was split: the captain had absolute authority in battle, but a quartermaster, elected by the men, controlled provisions, chose and shared out the loot, and judged quarrels and punishments. Articles required unanimous consent and were agreed before a voyage began. Why would thieves govern themselves like this? Two influential answers compete.

  • The labour-history reading. Marcus Rediker, a historian of sailors "from below", sees pirates as rebels against the violent, hierarchical merchant ships and Royal Navy they came from. In a 2020 interview he said pirates built "an egalitarian, democratic, multiracial social order",1 noted that many crews included runaways from plantations and black sailors, and argued that although pirates sometimes traded slaves, more often they freed enslaved Africans to join their crews.
  • The economic reading. The economist Peter Leeson, in a 2007 paper titled "An-arrgh-chy", treats pirates as rational criminals with a management problem. Crews averaged about 80 men, too many for one captain to watch, and a captain with unchecked power could cheat or abuse them. Elected quartermasters and written constitutions were checks and balances that kept the enterprise working. Leeson points out that this separation of powers came before its adoption by seventeenth- and eighteenth-century governments: France did not have one until 1789.2

The two readings share their evidence and differ on motive: ideals of fairness, or the cold logic of a profitable gang. Each has limits. Rediker himself says that many pirates were violent thugs, and Royal Museums Greenwich doubts that pirates often freed enslaved people, noting that they usually sold them once they reached land.3 Leeson explains the rules well but says less about the anger at brutal discipline that drove sailors to turn pirate. Both lean on Johnson's book and on trial records written by the men who hanged pirates. Perhaps both are right: a crew of free men needed fairness to stay together and profit to stay at sea.

title: Myth versus Evidence
description: Planks, buried treasure, eyepatches, 'arr' and the women pirates' trial

concepts.title: Walking the Plank and Buried Treasure
concepts.contentHtml:
Ask anyone how pirates killed their prisoners and you will hear about the plank: hands tied, a slow walk along a board over the sea. The evidence is thin. Royal Museums Greenwich says walking the plank happened "at least a few times" but that there are few documented instances,1 so it was probably not a regular practice; another page on the same museum's website says pirates never did it at all. The historian Colin Woodard calls it "pure Hollywood". When pirates wanted someone dead, it was easier to throw him overboard. Their documented punishments were grimmer and more practical, such as marooning, leaving an offender on a deserted island with a keg of water and a pistol, as well as beating, whipping and keelhauling.

Where did the plank come from? One ancient seed is Plutarch's report that Cilician pirates made Roman captives walk along a ladder into the sea. The modern picture was fixed by illustrators such as Howard Pyle and above all by J. M. Barrie2's Peter Pan, where it plays a starring role.

Buried treasure is almost entirely fiction too. Pirates spent their loot fast, in havens where drink, gambling and sex emptied purses quickly, and much of what they took was not coin at all. The usual booty was goods: timber, furs, silks, cotton, spices and medical supplies,3 plus cable, rigging and sails to keep their own ships afloat. Burying it would have been risky, with shifting sands and crewmates you could not trust.

There is one real exception, and it explains the legend. In 1699 Captain Kidd, hoping for a pardon, buried some treasure on Gardiner's Island near Long Island, New York.4 After his arrest at least some of it was dug up and sent to London as evidence for his trial. Because what was found did not match the loot he was thought to have taken, people assumed the rest must still be hidden, and treasure hunters have searched ever since. Kidd drew no map. The map where X marks the spot belongs to Robert Louis Stevenson's 1883 novel Treasure Island.

concepts.title: Eyepatches, Parrots and 'Arrr!'
concepts.contentHtml:
Some of the costume is real. Seafaring was dangerous, and pirate crews, like any sailors, included men with wooden legs or a lost eye. A sailor who had lost a limb often became the ship's cook, which is exactly the job Stevenson gave his one-legged Long John Silver. But Silver has no eyepatch in the book; later depictions added it.1 The swaggering outfits of bandanas, sashes and boots owe much to the American artist Howard Pyle, who took his inspiration from Spanish bandits of the late nineteenth century. Real eighteenth-century sailors wore loose trousers cut off at the knee and thigh-length blouses.

Parrots? Occasionally. Pirates followed trade routes, and exotic animals were trade goods. A parrot took up little space, was entertaining on a long voyage and could be sold for good money back home. Not every pirate had one, but they were not unheard of.

The voice is the newest invention of all. Disney's 1950 film of Treasure Island, the studio's first live-action feature, starred the Dorset-born actor Robert Newton as Silver.2 Newton exaggerated his own West Country accent, in which "arr" was an everyday word of agreement, and his "arrs", "shiver me timbers" and "landlubbers" shaped every screen pirate since. Real pirates spoke like other sailors of their day, and they came from everywhere. A sample of 700 pirates active in the Caribbean between 1715 and 1725 was 35 per cent English, 25 per cent American, 20 per cent West Indian, 10 per cent Scottish and 8 per cent Welsh,3 and Colin Woodard thinks the largest group of English pirates probably came from London, not the West Country. International Talk Like a Pirate Day, every 19 September, was dreamed up on an Oregon racquetball court in 1995.4

Even the Jolly Roger was less uniform than films suggest. Blackbeard's flag reportedly showed a skeleton aiming a spear at a bleeding heart, and a red flag could mean no quarter. Crews also carried other nations' flags so they could get close before revealing themselves.

concepts.title: Anne Bonny, Mary Read and the Trial Record
concepts.contentHtml:
Much of what people "know" about the golden age comes from one book: A General History of the Robberies and Murders of the Most Notorious Pyrates, first published in 1724 under the name Captain Charles Johnson. Nobody knows who Johnson was. In 1939 the scholar John Robert Moore attributed the book to Daniel Defoe,1 author of Robinson Crusoe, but that attribution is now largely rejected after work by Furbank and Owens from 1988, and Arne Bialuschewski has argued for Nathaniel Mist instead. Johnson clearly used trial papers and newspaper reports, and many of his statements check out against the records, but he also added and exaggerated to make a better story.

The two most famous women pirates show why that matters. Johnson gives Mary Read and Anne Bonny dramatic life stories, full of disguises, a soldier husband who died young and a failed tavern, which are hard to check. The trial is a different kind of source. In November 1720 a ship sent by the new governor of Jamaica surprised John "Calico Jack" Rackham's ship off the western tip of the island, and the crew was tried at St Jago de la Vega, now Spanish Town. Witnesses described both women in action. Thomas Dillon called them "both profligate, cursing and swearing much, and very ready and willing to do anything on board".2 A French witness, speaking through an interpreter, said that when they gave chase or attacked they wore men's clothes, and at other times women's clothes.

Both women were sentenced to hang, and both escaped the gallows for a while because they were pregnant. Read died of fever in prison in 1721.3 What became of Bonny is unknown, despite many confident later stories. The lesson applies to every pirate tale: separate what witnesses swore to at the time from what a writer later found too good to leave out. The trial shows that the women chose piracy and fought; the novelistic details rest mostly on Johnson alone.

title: Enemies of All Mankind: Endings and Today
description: Pardons and gallows, the law of piracy, and Somalia to the Singapore Strait

concepts.title: Pardons, Gallows and Gunboats
concepts.contentHtml:
The golden age ended with a deliberate campaign. By the late 1710s merchants and the British government were pressing colonial governors who had turned a blind eye to piracy, some because they profited from it. On 5 September 1717 King George I offered a pardon to pirates who gave up.1 The man sent to apply it was Woodes Rogers, a former privateer who had sailed round the world and rescued the castaway Alexander Selkirk, the inspiration for Defoe's Robinson Crusoe. Appointed the first royal governor of the Bahamas in 1717, he had only three armed ships, so the pardon was his best weapon: pirates who took it received a small plot of land on Providence Island instead of a rope. Many did; those who refused were hunted down.

The stick was the Royal Navy and the gallows. Hundreds of pirates were captured and publicly hanged from London to the Carolinas. In London they died at Execution Dock on the Thames, placed near the low-tide mark because that was the limit of the Admiralty's authority.2 A short rope meant the condemned usually strangled slowly. The bodies of notorious captains were tarred and hung in iron cages as warnings: Kidd's remains were visible to passing ships for two years.

The Barbary corsairs took longer to stop, and the young United States played an unexpected part. Once independent, American ships lost the Royal Navy's protection, and in 1785 Algiers declared war on the United States and captured several American ships. In 1794, in response to Algerian seizures, Congress authorised the first six ships of the US Navy.3 A 1795 treaty, which committed the United States to paying tribute, freed 83 American sailors. War with Tripoli followed in 1801–1805, and in 1815 Commodore Stephen Decatur forced Algiers to accept a treaty ending tribute and ransom. Even so, raiding in the Mediterranean resumed and, despite punitive British bombardments, did not stop until the French conquest of Algeria in 1830.

concepts.title: Hostis Humani Generis: The Oldest Universal Crime
concepts.contentHtml:
Remember Cicero's pirate, "the common foe of all the world"? English lawyers sharpened the idea. Blackstone's Commentaries, quoting Sir Edward Coke, called the pirate hostis humani generis, the enemy of the human race, and described piracy as "an offence against the universal law of society".1 In 1820 Justice Story, writing for the US Supreme Court in United States v. Smith, explained that the common law treated piracy as an offence against the law of nations, "a pirate being deemed an enemy of the human race.2" Because pirates attacked everyone on the open sea, where no state ruled, any state could punish them. That made piracy the classic crime of universal jurisdiction.

The modern rules sit in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea of 10 December 1982 (UNCLOS). Article 105 says that on the high seas, or anywhere outside any state's jurisdiction, every state may seize a pirate ship and arrest the people on board.3 Article 101 defines piracy narrowly, and each phrase matters:

  • "Any illegal acts of violence or detention, or any act of depredation": robbery, hijacking and kidnapping all count.
  • "Committed for private ends": acts carried out by states are excluded.
  • "By the crew or the passengers of a private ship": a warship counts only if its crew has mutinied and taken control (Article 102).
  • "On the high seas, against another ship": one vessel must attack another, so on this wording a hijacking by people already aboard is not piracy.

Geography matters as much as wording. Inside a state's internal waters, archipelagic waters or territorial sea, the International Maritime Organization classes the same act as armed robbery against ships, not piracy,4 and it falls to that state's own law. That is why the International Maritime Bureau reports "piracy and armed robbery" together: many incidents in its headline totals are not piracy in the legal sense at all.

concepts.title: Somalia, the Singapore Strait and Piracy Now
concepts.contentHtml:
Piracy never went away. In the late 2000s it surged off Somalia, where gangs used captured vessels as mother ships to hijack merchant ships far out to sea and hold their crews for ransom. In the first three months of 2011 the International Maritime Bureau (IMB) recorded 142 attacks worldwide, the highest first-quarter figure it had ever seen, 97 of them off Somalia.1 That year Somali pirates were behind 237 incidents, and 802 seafarers were taken hostage worldwide.

Then it collapsed: 75 Somali incidents in 2012 and just 15 in 2013, the fewest since 2006.2 The IMB credits a mix of measures: international navies, which struck pre-emptively at pirate mother ships; the "hardening" of merchant vessels under the industry's Best Management Practices; private armed security teams; and a steadier central government ashore. The last point echoes Pompey: patrols suppress piracy, but order and a living on land end it.

Success did not last. Because the threat seemed to have passed, the shipping industry rescinded its Indian Ocean High Risk Area from 1 January 2023. On 14 December 2023 the IMB recorded the first successful hijacking off Somalia since 2017,3 of a bulk carrier about 700 nautical miles east of Bosaso. In the first half of 2026 reported incidents worldwide fell to their lowest mid-year level since 1992, yet Somali pirates accounted for 94 per cent of all crew taken hostage, and four vessels were hijacked in the region in April and May.

In Asia the hotspot is the Singapore Strait, a narrow lane that the IMB says carries roughly 30 per cent of global trade. Incidents there rose from 43 in 2024 to 80 in 2025, more than half of all those reported worldwide.4 Most were low-level and opportunistic, but reports of guns rose from 8 to 27, and incidents fell sharply after Indonesian Marine Police caught two gangs in July 2025. Regional cooperation has a record too: ReCAAP, an agreement concluded by 16 Asian countries in November 2004 and in force since September 2006, runs an information-sharing centre that the International Maritime Organization holds up as a model.
